function.description: Simulates the creation of sea foam based on the agitation level of water, amount of organic material, and the presence of salt. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

agitation_level.description: The level of agitation in the water, represented by a scale from 1 (calm) to 10 (very agitated).

organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**What’s the Color of the Sea?** > In most places around the world, the sea appears **blue‑green**, though its hue shifts dramatically depending on conditions such as depth, sunlight, weather, and what’s dissolved or suspended in the water. | Factor | How it changes the appearance | |--------|------------------------------| | **Depth** | Shallow waters scatter more green light; deeper areas absorb red wavelengths so they look bluer. | | **Sunlight & Angle** | At noon the sun is high → clearer, brighter blues. Early morning or late afternoon gives warmer, golden tints because longer wavelengths dominate. | | **Water Composition** |
  • Clear seawater – deep blue.
  • Sandy bottoms – turquoise / teal.
  • Algal blooms – greenish or even brownish if dense.
| | **Atmospheric Conditions** | Overcast skies reduce glare, making the surface appear darker; clear skies give a vivid sky reflection. | | **Distance & Perspective** | From afar you see a uniform blue; up close you notice ripples, waves, and subtle variations. | ### Why Blue‑Green? Seawater absorbs long‑wavelength reds, oranges, and yellows very efficiently while scattering shorter blue wavelengths. That selective absorption + Rayleigh scattering produces the classic “ocean” color we’re accustomed to seeing—especially when looking at open water away from shorelines. --- So next time you stare out over the horizon, remember: the sea isn’t just one single shade—it’s a dynamic palette shaped by physics, biology, and atmosphere!
